clue.text: New financial institution losing pounds over a quarter

indicators.note: over in a down-or-across sense of turning something over, so the trimmed institution is read backwards
losing says the pounds abbreviation is dropped from the institution

parts.note: a mutual is a building society or insurer owned by its members
L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling (from Latin libra)

explanation.surface: A newly founded bank has lost a lot of money over three months of trading.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' and 'over' work on the building-society word; 'a quarter' looks like part of the financial story but is the definition, a season.
explanation.definitionFit: Autumn is one of the four seasons, each of which takes up a quarter of the year.

clue.text: Kidnapper's muscle

definitions.meaning: one who abducts, or kidnaps, a person
a muscle that draws a limb away from the body's midline

explanation.surface: A kidnapper's brawn.
explanation.definitionFit: Abduction means both carrying off a person and moving a limb outward, so both senses share one noun.

clue.text: Nuisance not having answer: girl in quandary

indicators.note: not having says the answer abbreviation is removed from the nuisance

parts.note: a trial is a trying person or thing, a nuisance
Emma is a girl's name

explanation.surface: An annoying person without a solution leaves a girl in a fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not having' takes A from TRIAL, leaving TRIL, then EMMA is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A trilemma is a dilemma with three options, all of them unattractive, so a predicament.

clue.text: Athlete who looks happy, though not first

indicators.note: not first means the opening letter of the happy person is dropped

parts.note: a smiler is a person who looks happy

explanation.surface: A sportsman who looks cheerful despite not winning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not first' looks like a race result but removes the S from SMILER.
explanation.definitionFit: A miler is a runner who specialises in the one-mile race.

clue.text: Wine sent spilling over cat

indicators.note: over here means lying across, so the scrambled letters sit around the cat
spilling suggests the letters of sent tumbling out of order

parts.note: the puma is a big American cat

explanation.surface: Someone's wine has been knocked over and spilt across the cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spilling' scrambles the letters of 'sent' to S…NTE, and 'over' lays them around the big cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Spumante is a sparkling Italian white, such as Asti.

clue.text: In distress, broken by temperature, leave the Badlands

indicators.note: broken by says the first word is split open with the temperature letter inside

parts.note: pained means hurt or in distress
to desert is to leave or abandon

explanation.surface: Someone upset by the heat abandons the barren wastes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken by' splits the distress word with T. The Badlands are a type of eroded terrain, not only the South Dakota park.
explanation.definitionFit: The Painted Desert is an area of eroded, colourful badlands in Arizona.

clue.text: Second royal in unpleasant house, a single-sex one

parts.note: a mo is a moment or second, as in 'just a mo'

indicators.note: in says the royal sits inside the unpleasant word

parts.note: nasty means unpleasant
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword royal

explanation.surface: A minor royal turns up at a nasty single-sex establishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the royal inside the unpleasant word. 'house' is the definition, qualified as a single-sex one: a religious house.
explanation.definitionFit: A monastery is a religious house where monks live, an all-male community.

clue.text: American politician's one foul trick

indicators.note: foul suggests something fouled up and in disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: a con is a confidence trick

explanation.surface: A US politician is accused of a dirty trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'foul' rearranges ONE to NEO, then CON is added.
explanation.definitionFit: A neocon, short for neoconservative, is a hawkish right-wing figure in US politics.

clue.text: Predator of rat, say, biting its head off and beginning to eat

indicators.note: biting its head off says the first letter of the vermin word is dropped

parts.note: rats are an example of vermin

indicators.note: beginning to means only the opening letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A predator bites the head off a rat before starting to eat it.
explanation.walkthrough: VERMIN loses its V to leave ERMIN, then E comes from the start of 'eat'.
explanation.definitionFit: The ermine is the stoat in its white winter coat, a small carnivore that hunts rodents.

clue.text: Case of 'Physician, heal thyself'? That's a bore

definitions.meaning: a sick doctor, ..., is the case where a physician must heal himself

explanation.surface: Someone groans that the proverb about a doctor curing himself is tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the answer as DR (doctor) and ILL: a physician who is ill is just the case the proverb describes.
explanation.definitionFit: A drill is a boring tool, and a bore can also mean the tool that makes a hole.

clue.text: Minor crag blasted for stone

indicators.note: rock that is blasted is blown apart, so these letters are scattered and reassembled

explanation.surface: A small rocky outcrop has been dynamited for building stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blasted' rearranges MINOR CRAG; the quarrying surface hides that the stone is a gem.
explanation.definitionFit: Cairngorm is a smoky brown quartz gemstone named after the Scottish mountains where it is found.

clue.text: Not a single job in Scottish island: a premature cancellation all round

parts.note: Coll is an island in the Inner Hebrides

indicators.note: all round says the cancellation word goes around the single letter

parts.note: an abortion is a project or mission called off early

explanation.surface: A one-off job on a Hebridean island is called off early.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all round' wraps the cancellation word around A. 'Not a single job' reads as a complaint about unemployment but means joint work.
explanation.definitionFit: A collaboration is work done jointly, so it is not something one person does alone.

clue.text: Coming to a point, band finally abandoned hire car

indicators.note: finally abandoned means the last letter of the band word is thrown away

parts.note: a chevron is a V-shaped stripe or band that comes to a point
to let is to hire out, as a flat or a car

explanation.surface: As things came to a head, the band gave up its rental car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally abandoned' drops the N from CHEVRON, giving CHEVRO, then LET is added.
explanation.definitionFit: Chevrolet is an American make of automobile, so a car by brand.

clue.text: Can it have to be proved?

parts.note: can it! is slang for be quiet, the same as sh!
to own something is to have it

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a tin can has to be proven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can it' reads like a question about a container, but it is the command to shut up, SH.
explanation.definitionFit: Shown and proved are both past participles meaning demonstrated to be true.

clue.text: Extravagantly commend a fine story

indicators.note: extravagantly suggests going wildly beyond bounds, so these letters are rearranged freely

explanation.surface: A reviewer heaps lavish praise on a good short story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extravagantly' rearranges COMMEND A FINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Of Mice and Men is John Steinbeck's 1937 novella, a short work of fiction.

clue.text: Final move of lover from Brno announced

indicators.note: announced means the phrase is spoken out loud, giving a word of the same sound

parts.note: Brno is a city in the Czech Republic, so a lover from there is a Czech mate

explanation.surface: Someone's last move is to declare a lover from a Czech city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'announced' turns 'Czech mate' into the chess term that sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Checkmate is the winning move that ends a game of chess.

clue.text: Curler, black, certainly fits round front of wig

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils

indicators.note: fits round says the certainty word is placed around the letter from the wig

parts.note: indeed means certainly

indicators.note: front of means only the first letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A black hair curler certainly fits round the edge of a wig.
explanation.walkthrough: W, the front of 'wig', goes inside INDEED, after B. 'Curler' suggests a hair roller but is a twining plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Bindweed is a climbing weed whose stems coil tightly around other plants.

clue.text: God! Imogen's work left in the wrong place

indicators.note: in the wrong place says the letter for left has been moved within the phrase

parts.note: Imogen, the setter, is a woman, so her work in this puzzle is her clues

explanation.surface: An exclamation of dismay that the setter's work has been mislaid.
explanation.walkthrough: Imogen's work is HER CLUES; moving the L to another place gives the answer. 'God!' looks like an oath but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hercules is the Roman form of Heracles, the hero made a god after his death.

clue.text: After some bowling on ground, I'm yet to get some spin: wait before able to perform again

definitions.text: wait before able to perform again

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed after, so the bowling follows the ground
after says the spun letters come later than the cricket pieces

parts.note: a rec is a recreation ground, a British public sports field
an over is a set of six balls bowled in cricket

indicators.note: spin, as a bowler puts on a ball, signals the letters being turned about

explanation.surface: A cricketer has bowled some overs and still needs to practise spin before playing again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get some spin' rearranges I'M YET to YTIME. REC is a recreation ground and an OVER is six balls in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Recovery time is the rest period an athlete or performer needs before returning to action.

clue.text: Mistakes of bosses seeing no resistance

indicators.note: seeing no says the resistance letter is now absent from the bosses

parts.note: gaffers is British slang for bosses or foremen
R is the physics symbol for resistance

explanation.surface: Bosses make errors when nobody stands up to them.
explanation.walkthrough: GAFFERS loses its R. A gaffer is British slang for a boss.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaffes are social blunders or embarrassing errors.

clue.text: Winner of an inaccurate timepiece?

definitions.meaning: one who gains, or comes out ahead
a clock that gains runs fast

explanation.surface: Someone wins a clock that doesn't keep good time.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaining is both getting ahead and, of a clock, running fast, so both senses fit one noun.

clue.text: Some black cab always around, so taken unexpectedly

indicators.note: around signals that the hidden run is read turning back on itself
some means only part of the letters of these words is taken

explanation.surface: Some London black cabs are always going round in circles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes a run of letters from 'black cab always' and 'around' reverses them: ...sYAWLABACKcalb. The answer completes the phrase 'taken aback'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be taken aback is to be surprised, caught off guard by something unforeseen.

clue.text: Irregular school lesson in fine class girl missed

indicators.note: in tells us the lesson sits inside the fine-class letters

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, written with I for the digit one
a period is a timetabled lesson at school

indicators.note: missed says the girl is taken out of the word class

parts.note: taken as the word class
a lass is a girl, especially in northern Britain and Scotland

explanation.surface: A girl skipped a lesson in a high-achieving class at school.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 (first-rate) gives AI; 'missed' takes LASS from CLASS, leaving C; PERIOD goes 'in' to make A-PERIOD-IC.
explanation.definitionFit: Aperiodic means not occurring at regular intervals, hence irregular.

clue.text: One magnet's orientation to hold copper for anvil

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: to hold says the orientation letters go round the copper

parts.note: a magnet has a north and a south pole, N and S
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A magnet is pointed so it can grip copper on a blacksmith's anvil.
explanation.walkthrough: I, then N and S around CU. 'anvil' suggests a smithy but is the ear bone.
explanation.definitionFit: The incus is the small anvil-shaped bone of the middle ear; its Latin name means anvil.

clue.text: One with a dream lover posed from behind first

parts.note: a fan is a lover or devotee of something

indicators.note: from behind means the word for posed is read from its end

parts.note: sat, as a model sits or poses for an artist
1st is the abbreviation for first, read as IST

explanation.surface: A dreamy admirer modelled for a portrait, and came at it from behind.
explanation.walkthrough: SAT is reversed by 'from behind' to give TAS; IST is 1ST with the digit read as I.
explanation.definitionFit: A fantasist lives in a world of daydreams and imagined scenarios.

clue.text: Native American's large basket

parts.note: the Cree are a Native American and First Nations people
L is the standard abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A big woven basket made by a Native American craftsperson.
explanation.definitionFit: A creel is a wicker basket, especially one an angler uses for fish.

clue.text: Colonist put on fabric, one with stripes

indicators.note: in an across answer put on means placed after, so the colonist follows the fabric

parts.note: serge is a hard-wearing twilled cloth
an ant lives in a colony, so is a colonist

explanation.surface: A settler dresses in cloth, perhaps a striped one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colonist' is an ant, a member of an insect colony, not a settler.
explanation.definitionFit: A sergeant wears three chevrons on the sleeve, so is a soldier with stripes.

clue.text: They are not generally to be heard speaking

definitions.text: They are not generally to be heard speaking

parts.words: They are not generally to be heard speaking
parts.note: stage remarks the audience hears but other characters supposedly do not

explanation.surface: A remark about things one usually cannot hear people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'generally' is the twist: these remarks are heard by the audience, but not by the general cast on stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Asides are lines an actor speaks to the audience, which other characters are imagined not to hear.
